title: DSA in Python: linked lists, trees and heaps
seriesDescription: Hashing, windows, stacks, binary search, lists, trees, heaps and graphs with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Python versions of linked list, tree and heap problems: iterative reversal, level order with deque, LCA, heapq top-k and tie-breaking, and an LRU cache on OrderedDict.
source: Python documentation (heapq, collections.deque, OrderedDict); LeetCode problem set; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `reverse(head)` that reverses a singly linked list iteratively (each node has `val and next` attributes) and returns the new head.

checks.label: loops while the current node is not None
saves the next node before rewiring
points the current node back to the previous one
returns the previous pointer as the new head

questions.model:
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev
questions.explanation: Save next first, or you lose the rest of the list. The loop runs n times with O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `lca(root, p, q)` returning the lowest common ancestor of nodes `p` and `q` in a binary tree (both exist; compare nodes with `is`).

checks.label: returns root on null or when root is p or q
recurses into the left subtree
recurses into the right subtree
returns root when both sides found something

questions.explanation: If p and q are found in different subtrees the current node is their meeting point; if only one side finds anything, bubble that result up. O(n) time, O(h) stack.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function `top_k_frequent(nums, k)` that returns the k most frequent values using `collections.Counter` and the `heapq` module.

checks.label: counts frequencies with Counter
uses heapq (nlargest or a size-k heap with heappush)
orders by the count, e.g. key=count.get or (count, value) tuples
returns the selected values

questions.explanation: nlargest with a key runs in O(n log k). A manual size-k min-heap of (count, value) tuples, or bucket sort by count (O(n)), is equivalent.

questions.explanation: `OrderedDict` is a hash map plus a doubly linked list underneath, which is exactly the textbook design. In an interview you may be asked to build the map and linked list by hand.

questions.prompt: Values `9, 4, 7, 1, 6, 2` are pushed onto an empty list with `heapq.heappush` in that order, then `heappop` is called twice. What does `h[0]` hold?
questions.explanation: The two pops remove 1 and 2, the smallest values. The remaining values are `4, 6, 7 and 9`, so the root is 4. I ran it to confirm.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Merging K sorted lists with N total nodes using a heap of list heads costs O(N log K).
questions.reason: The heap can grow to hold all N nodes at the same time.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option applies.
whys.c: Correct: A is true and the heap holds at most K entries (one head per list), so R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Each of the N nodes is pushed and popped once at O(log K). `heapq.merge` does this lazily for sorted iterables.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: `heapq.heapify(xs)` turns a list of n items into a heap in O(n) time.
questions.reason: Half of the nodes of a binary heap are leaves, and heapify sifts down only from the internal nodes.

whys.a: Correct: most nodes sit near the bottom and travel only a short distance, so the sum of work is linear.
whys.b: R is the reason for the linear bound, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Heapify is O(n); n separate `heappush` calls are O(n log n). Use heapify when you already have all the data.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: `heapq.nsmallest(k, xs)` runs in O(n log k) time for small k.
questions.reason: The `heapq` functions operate on plain Python lists.

whys.a: R has nothing to do with the log k factor.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but working on plain lists does not explain the bound; the log k comes from keeping a heap of only k candidates.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: For k close to n, simply sorting is as good. For k = 1 use `min()`.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Printing the list behind a `heapq` heap shows its items in sorted order.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: R is true, but the list is only heap-ordered: pushing 5, 3, 8, 1 leaves [1, 3, 8, 5].

questions.explanation: Pop repeatedly (or `sorted(h)`) when you need sorted output. I ran the `5, 3, 8, 1` example and got `[1, 3, 8, 5]`.

questions.prompt: Match each heapq call with its behaviour.

right.text: Adds x and restores the heap order in O(log n)
Removes and returns the smallest item
Pushes x first, then pops and returns the smallest, in one step
Pops the smallest first, then pushes x (it raises on an empty heap)
Returns the k biggest items in descending order
Returns the items in sorted order in O(n)

questions.explanation: heappushpop and heapreplace are the efficient building blocks of a size-k heap; the difference is whether the push or the pop comes first.

questions.prompt: You push `(priority, node)` tuples onto a `heapq` heap, where `node` is a custom object without ordering methods. What can go wrong when two entries have the same priority?

options.text: Python compares the nodes, so a `TypeError` is raised.
options.why: Correct: tuple comparison falls through to the nodes, and objects without ordering cannot be compared.

options.text: The heap silently drops one of the two equal entries.
options.why: Heaps never drop items; equal priorities are both kept.

options.text: `heappush` sorts the whole list again, ruining the O(log n) cost of a push.
options.why: `heappush` sifts one item only; it never re-sorts the list.

options.text: The entry with the larger node object always pops first.
options.why: Node objects cannot be ordered, so there is no such rule.

questions.explanation: Add a unique counter as a tie-breaker: `(priority, next(counter), node)`. I ran the failing case and got the `TypeError`.

questions.text: To keep the k largest numbers, hold a {1}-heap of size {2}; after each heappush, if len(h) > k call {3} to drop the smallest.
questions.explanation: `heapq` only provides a min-heap, which is what this recipe needs. For a max-heap negate the values.

questions.prompt: In a list maintained with `heapq`, `h[0]` is always the smallest item.

options.why: Correct: the heap invariant puts the minimum at index 0.
The heap invariant guarantees exactly this.

questions.explanation: Peeking at `h[0]` is O(1); `heappop` is O(log n).

questions.prompt: Appending to a list with `list.append` keeps it a valid `heapq` heap, so `heappop` still returns the smallest item.

options.why: `append` does not sift the new item into place.
Correct: only `heappush` maintains the heap invariant; after a raw `append` the order is not guaranteed.

questions.explanation: If you build the list by hand, call `heapq.heapify(list)` once afterwards.
